title: Aura
tagline: An ambient companion that lives on the shelf, not in your pocket.
imageAlt: The Aura speaker — a matte black body with a glossy red arch handle
lede: Designing a voice companion people actually want in the living room.
overview: Smart speakers won the countertop and lost the heart. Aura started from a different question: what if the object itself invited touch? We shaped the hardware language, the packaging, and the setup flow around one glossy red handle — a single gesture that says pick me up. Every screen in the companion app answers to the physical product, not the other way round.
problem: Voice assistants had become invisible utilities — black cylinders people hide behind plants. Nothing about the category said companionship, and setup flows buried the delight under permissions and pairing spinners.
solution: One bold gesture: the arch. The handle became the brand, the app icon, and the onboarding motif. Setup was cut from eleven steps to four, and the first thing Aura does out of the box is say hello — before you sign in to anything.

title: Ledger
tagline: A vault you can hold — cold storage without the cold sweat.
imageAlt: A brushed titanium hardware wallet resting on a dark surface
lede: Making self-custody feel as solid as the metal it ships in.
overview: Hardware wallets ask ordinary people to behave like security engineers. Ledger's brief was to move the confidence from the manual into the object. We paired a machined titanium slab with an interface that never shows a hex string unless you ask for one — balances, recovery, and signing all speak plain language first.
problem: Every existing flow treated the seed phrase ceremony as a test the user could fail. One mistyped word and people abandoned the product — or worse, photographed the phrase.
solution: A guided recovery ritual with physical checkpoints: the device confirms each word back on its own screen, the app never sees it, and the packaging doubles as the backup template. Support tickets about recovery dropped to near zero in beta.

title: Stride
tagline: A running coach that respects the run.
imageAlt: The Stride band standing upright with its green accent ring
lede: Stripping a fitness tracker back to the three numbers runners feel.
overview: Stride's founders came with a paradox: their band collected forty metrics and their users looked at three. We rebuilt the product around pace, effort, and streak — everything else moved behind one deliberate tap. The band's single green ring became the whole status language: solid when you are on plan, breathing when it is rest day.
problem: The old dashboard was a cockpit. Runners mid-workout could not parse it at arm's length, and the post-run summary buried the one question that matters — was that better than last time?
solution: A glanceable mid-run screen with type sized for motion, a post-run story that leads with the comparison, and notifications that never interrupt a run in progress. Weekly retention rose 22% in the redesign cohort.

title: Verse
tagline: A writing partner that knows when to stay quiet.
imageAlt: A polished chrome knot sculpture floating over a pale ground
lede: Interface patterns for AI that assists without taking the pen.
overview: Verse is a drafting tool for people who like writing. The founding constraint: the model may never type into the document. We designed a margin where suggestions wait — quiet, collapsed, dismissible with one key — and a review mode that shows the writer exactly what changed and why. The knot became our metaphor: ideas intertwined, never tangled.
problem: Early testers described AI writing tools as a co-author who grabs the keyboard. Acceptance rates looked healthy while trust cratered — people shipped text they could not defend.
solution: Suggestions live beside the text, not inside it. Each one carries its reasoning in a single sentence, and accepting is an edit the writer performs. Trust scores doubled, and the accept rate barely moved — which was exactly the point.
